Markuszow New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Markuszów, Poland

Not demolished. Markuszów's newer Jewish cemetery, established around the turn of the 19th century roughly 700 meters from its predecessor (documented in a companion record elsewhere in this collection), was enlarged in 1937 and enclosed with a concrete fence; the town was bombed at the start of WWII, including this cemetery, and victims of two mass executions in 1942 and 1943 were buried here. Its matzevot were used for construction — pavements, stairs, thresholds — both during and after the war, and in the 1970s the site was used for livestock grazing and informal gatherings before entering Poland's Register of Monuments in 1989. In August 2016, a cleanup effort brought together the family of Dan Oren, volunteers from the American Matzevah Foundation, and Poland's Studnia Pamięci Association; research across the 1990s and 2016 has documented around 160 surviving objects, including 68 matzevot, 89 flat tombstones, and 2 mass graves, with the three oldest dated tombstones — from 1847, 1853, and 1855 — now marked by a monument erected by the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage in Poland. The site has begun to grow overgrown again since the 2016 restoration.
